headline: Apple Says It Has Proof That a Former Worker Took Secrets to OpenAI

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Apple is a company that makes phones and computers. Apple thinks a man named Chang Liu, who used to work there, took secret company information with him when he left. Now Liu works for a different company called OpenAI, which builds computer programs. Apple says Liu used Apple's private plans and tools to help OpenAI, which is not allowed. This is called stealing 'trade secrets,' which means private information a company keeps hidden so other companies cannot copy their ideas. Apple looked at Liu's old work laptop and says they found strong proof he did this. Apple also says another OpenAI worker tried to help delete evidence. OpenAI says Liu only helped old coworkers by accident, and that it was Apple's own mistake for not locking him out sooner. Apple wants a judge to stop OpenAI from using this information while everyone figures out what really happened. This matters because it shows how important it is for companies to protect their private ideas, just like you might want to protect a secret recipe or a private journal.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Apple, the technology company known for iPhones and Mac computers, is suing OpenAI, a company that builds artificial intelligence tools. Apple believes a former employee named Chang Liu stole secret company information, called trade secrets, and used it in his new job at OpenAI. Trade secrets are private designs, plans, or tools that a company does not want competitors to see, because they took time and money to create. Apple says its lawyers found 'shocking evidence' after getting Liu's old work laptop, including a private circuit design and a tool with the same name as an internal Apple program. Apple also claims Liu got a coworker to help destroy proof once he learned he was being investigated. OpenAI disagrees, saying Liu only helped old coworkers after leaving Apple and that this happens because Apple is not careful about shutting off former employees' access. Apple says Liu actually found and used a rare security weakness to keep getting into Apple's systems. Because of all this, Apple is asking a judge to temporarily stop OpenAI from building any technology based on Apple's ideas until the case is settled. Apple also wants to quickly gather more evidence, since it says over 400 former Apple workers now work at OpenAI, and some of them might also be involved. This case matters because it shows how competition between big tech companies can lead to serious legal fights over stolen ideas and data.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Apple and OpenAI, two major technology companies, are locked in a legal battle over accusations of stolen trade secrets. Apple claims that a former employee, Chang Liu, who now works at OpenAI, secretly used confidential Apple information to benefit his new employer. Trade secrets are protected pieces of information, like designs or software tools, that give a company an advantage over competitors. Losing control of them can hurt a company's ability to compete and can cost it money and reputation. Apple says it recently obtained Liu's old work laptop and found strong evidence, including a private circuit design and a program sharing a name with an internal Apple engineering tool. Apple also alleges that when Liu found out he was under investigation, he asked a colleague at OpenAI to help destroy proof of what he had done. OpenAI, however, argues that Liu only accessed old files to help former coworkers who reached out to him after he left Apple, and that any lingering access was caused by Apple's own failure to properly cancel his account permissions when he departed. Apple disputes this explanation, claiming Liu instead exploited an unusual and previously unknown flaw in its security systems to keep secretly viewing company data. Because of these serious accusations, Apple is asking a judge for a preliminary injunction, a court order that would immediately stop OpenAI from developing any hardware based on Apple's technology while the lawsuit continues. Apple is also requesting expedited discovery, meaning a faster legal process for collecting evidence, because it suspects that many more of the over 400 former Apple employees now working at OpenAI could be involved in similar misconduct. This case highlights growing tensions in the technology industry, where fierce competition for talent and innovation can sometimes blur the line between fair hiring and unfair corporate espionage. It also raises questions about how well companies protect sensitive data when employees move between rival firms, and how the legal system determines who is responsible when private information ends up in the wrong hands.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Apple has escalated its lawsuit against OpenAI by submitting what it describes as 'shocking evidence' supporting claims that a former employee misused confidential company information. The dispute centers on Chang Liu, who left Apple and now works at OpenAI, a leading artificial intelligence company. According to Apple, after weeks of delay, Liu's legal team finally handed over his old Apple work laptop for inspection. Apple's lawyers say the device revealed that Liu had used a confidential Apple circuit schematic, essentially a technical blueprint for hardware, along with a software tool sharing a name with an internal Apple engineering application. Apple further alleges that OpenAI knew Liu still had access to this sensitive information and that, once Liu learned he was under investigation, he recruited a colleague, Yu-Ting Peng, to help destroy evidence. Earlier court filings reportedly included text messages in which Liu appeared to joke about still having access to Apple's internal files. OpenAI has pushed back, arguing that Liu only helped former coworkers with lingering technical questions after leaving Apple, and that any continued access to files resulted from Apple's own carelessness in revoking employee permissions, something OpenAI claims is a common problem at Apple. Apple rejects this defense, insisting that Liu instead exploited a rare and previously undiscovered flaw in its authentication systems, essentially a hidden security loophole, to intentionally maintain unauthorized access long after his employment ended. Because of the severity of these allegations, Apple is requesting a preliminary injunction, a legal order that would immediately prevent OpenAI from continuing hardware development based on any of Apple's proprietary technology while the case proceeds. Apple is also seeking expedited discovery, an accelerated evidence-gathering process, citing concern that additional former employees may be similarly involved. Notably, Apple's court filings state that more than 400 former Apple workers currently work at OpenAI, raising questions about how much protected knowledge may have transferred between the companies. This case reflects broader tensions within the technology sector, where rapid movement of skilled engineers between competing firms, especially in the booming AI industry, creates real risks around intellectual property protection. It also underscores how difficult it can be to enforce clear boundaries around confidential information once employees change jobs, and how legal systems attempt to balance protecting corporate secrets with allowing normal career mobility.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: Apple's ongoing legal battle against OpenAI has intensified with the submission of what Apple calls 'shocking evidence' meant to substantiate its claims that a former employee misappropriated trade secrets for the benefit of a competitor. The case centers on Chang Liu, a former Apple employee now working at OpenAI, whose legal representatives recently surrendered his old company laptop for forensic review after weeks of delay. Apple contends that analysis of the device revealed Liu had used a confidential Apple circuit schematic, a detailed technical diagram for hardware design, as well as a software tool bearing the same name as an internal Apple engineering application. Apple further alleges that OpenAI was aware Liu retained unauthorized access to this proprietary information, and that once Liu learned he was under internal investigation, he enlisted a colleague, Yu-Ting Peng, to help destroy incriminating evidence. Previous filings reportedly included text messages in which Liu, punctuating his messages with laughing emojis, appeared to casually acknowledge that he still had access to Apple's internal systems. OpenAI has consistently defended Liu, asserting that he only accessed old files to assist former coworkers who reached out for technical help after his departure, and that any continued access stemmed from Apple's own inadequate offboarding procedures, a problem OpenAI characterizes as a recurring issue at Apple. Apple firmly disputes this narrative, alleging instead that Liu deliberately exploited a rare, previously unknown vulnerability in its authentication systems, effectively a hidden flaw in its security infrastructure, to sustain unauthorized access well after leaving the company. Given the gravity of these accusations, Apple is seeking a preliminary injunction, a court order that would immediately halt OpenAI's development of hardware based on any Apple-derived technology while litigation proceeds. Apple has also requested expedited discovery, an accelerated legal process for evidence collection, citing concern that a broader pattern of misconduct may involve additional former employees. Strikingly, Apple's original filing notes that more than 400 former Apple employees currently work at OpenAI, a statistic that raises significant questions about the porous boundaries between competing firms in the fast-moving technology and artificial intelligence sectors. Beyond the specifics of this individual case, the dispute illuminates larger structural tensions within the tech industry: the intense competition for specialized engineering talent, the challenges companies face in safeguarding proprietary information as employees migrate between rivals, and the legal system's ongoing struggle to balance protection of corporate intellectual property against individuals' rights to pursue new employment. As artificial intelligence companies increasingly compete to build advanced hardware and software, cases like this may set important precedents for how trade secret law applies to the modern, highly mobile tech workforce.

questions: If you found out that something private of yours, like a school project or personal notes, ended up being used by someone else without your permission, how would you feel, and what do you think should happen next?

Why do you think it's important for organizations, like schools or companies, to make sure people lose access to accounts and files once they leave? Can you think of examples from your own school experience?
Do you think it's fair to blame a company for a security mistake if it made it easier for someone to take information without permission? Why or why not?
